item.title: CVS is splitting into two companies: Healthcare giant’s ‘Pharmacy’ breakup explained
item.description:
CVS is breaking up.

On Wednesday, the healthcare giant announced plans to split into two separate, independent companies, and both will be publicly traded. 

The two companies will form a “leading healthcare solutions company” called CVS Health, and will encompass Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.

The second company, dubbed CVS Pharmacy, will be made up of roughly 9,000 CVS pharmacies, mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic, and the Health100 tech services business.

The company also announced that current CVS Health chair and CEO David Joyner will serve as CEO of the “new” CVS Health, and Prem Shah, current Group President of CVS Health, will be the CEO of the “new” CVS Pharmacy.

“Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access, and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement. “From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination.”

CVS shares were down approximately 12% on Wednesday morning.

As for the reason for the split?

Notably, the move effectively reverses, in some respects, the 2018 merger between CVS Health and Aetna.

According to company leadership, two smaller companies would be able to be more efficient and nimble than one single, larger one. When the dust settles, CVS Pharmacy will basically be a pharmacy company, while CVS Health will be focused on insurance and other services.

Regulatory concerns may also be at play. For example, The New York Times reports that some states, such as Arkansas and Tennessee, have passed laws in recent years that prevent large conglomerates from managing prescription benefits while simultaneously running retail and mail-order pharmacy services. 

Other companies have taken on similar strategies in recent years. Notably, Comcast is breaking off its media and technology businesses, it announced earlier this year, which likewise follows NBCUniversal’s decision to spin off some of its brands into another company, Versant.

Further, Madison Square Garden Sports is spinning off its pro sports franchises (the NHL’s New York Rangers and the NBA’s New York Knicks) into separate companies. And Keurig Dr Pepper recently announced plans to spin off its coffee division.

item.title: Google announces it will cut off internet search access for schools that reject AI
item.description:
Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company’s search engine unless their school system also opts in to using artificial intelligence, the tech giant said Tuesday.

The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.

On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators. Instead, K-12 schools will be able to individually turn each Google tool on or off — including Gemini, Gemini Notebook and search, with each being off by default until administrators turn it on. But because search is integrated with AI, schools that opt out of AI altogether would also lose access to Google search.

“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.

The company also said it is updating its search tools to make them “better for learning,” including offering step-by-step guided learning through problems, so that students don’t get quick answers to schoolwork.”

But turning off AI altogether is not possible if schools want to use Google products.

Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform, and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.

Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

Tuesday’s announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.

“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation’s biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.

Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development.

Josh Golin, executive director of children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said Google’s attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google’s technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.

“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available,” Golin said in a statement.

Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and “use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

—Barbara Ortutay, AP Technology Writer

item.title: Jack Dorsey’s Block is cutting jobs again. Here’s what makes these layoffs different
item.description:
Jack Dorsey’s fintech company, Block, began a second round of layoffs on Wednesday, months after cutting more than 4,000 jobs in February. The company has not said how many employees are affected at this time. 

The cuts hit the Customer Ops, Risk Ops, and Learning & Content Operations teams supporting Cash App, Block’s consumer financial services app, and Square, its tool for sellers. According to Business Insider, those teams will be “reducing the number of roles, changing some responsibilities, and shifting some reporting lines.” 

Affected employees are expected to receive a “separation package and transition support, similar to those affected in February 2026.” Block has not detailed the new terms. In February, laid-off employees received 20 weeks of severance or more, depending on their tenure, equity vested until the end of May, six months of healthcare, any corporate devices, and an extra $5,000. 

Block did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment as of publication. 

The layoffs came one day after Block reported its third-quarter results on Tuesday. The company said it raised its 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, up from its initial $12.51 billion estimate. It also projected fourth-quarter gross profit of $3.32 billion. 

Block hasn’t explained what drove this round of layoffs. Earlier this year, Dorsey announced that the February layoffs were not because of financial issues, but because of “intelligence tools,” like AI.

“A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better,” Dorsey wrote on X. “Intelligence tool capabilities are compounding faster every week.”

“We see an opportunity to move faster with smaller, highly talented teams using AI to automate more work,” Block CFO Amrita Ahuja said. 

Block is also continuing to build its own AI products. The company recently released Dessa, a speech-to-speech AI voice model trained on the recording of real human conversations.

item.title: Nintendo reports profit is up 11%, but sales slipped for the first half of the fiscal year
item.description:
Japanese video-game maker Nintendo reported Thursday an 11% improvement in its net profit in the first half of the fiscal year, although its sales declined during that period.

Kyoto-based Nintendo Co.’s April-September profit rose to 220.9 billion yen ($1.4 billion) from nearly 199 billion yen in the same period a year earlier. Sales during the six months slipped 12% to 966 billion yen.

Nintendo, which makes Pokemon, Super Mario and Legend of Zelda games, sold 1.27 million Switch game consoles during the six months, and 6.49 million of its Switch 2 machines, the company said.

In game software, “Star Fox” and “Splatoon Raiders,” released during that period, sold briskly, while earlier releases like “Mario Kart World” were still in demand, it said.

Nintendo’s digital sales, including proceeds from downloadable games, continued to surge. The popularity of “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie,” a 2026 animation film, also boosted its bottom line.

Companies like Nintendo tend to record their biggest sales during the present-giving Christmas and New Year’s seasons.

Nintendo did not break down quarterly details. It kept its projections for the full fiscal year through March 2027 unchanged at 310 billion yen profit, down nearly 27% from the previous fiscal year, on 2 trillion yen in sales, down 11%.

Like other technology companies, Nintendo is facing the problem of a computer chips crunch and surging prices due to the recent global boom in artificial intelligence.

Nintendo stocks rose 6.3% Thursday in Tokyo.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Russia has damaged ‘every power plant’ as he seeks Latin American help
item.description:
Ukraine president tells leaders Kyiv needs equipment for its power grid – ‘and we need it fast’. Donald Trump predicts ‘very big’ deal with Russia. What we know on day 1,717

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged Latin American leaders to help Ukraine obtain urgently needed equipment to repair its power infrastructure damaged by Russian strikes. “Every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged in one way or another by attacks,” the Ukrainian president said at a summit in Madrid on Thursday, adding that repair crews were working around the clock. “We need as much international cooperation as possible to continue rebuilding and repairing our energy system,” he told a meeting on the sidelines of a summit of the Ibero-American Community, a 22-nation group of mainly Latin American Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries. “We know that companies in Spain and Latin America can help with this, can support this,” Zelenskyy said. “We need equipment that works with our power grid, and we need it fast.”

Donald Trump predicted a “very big” deal with Russia involving not only the Ukraine war but “all of Europe”, after meeting Russian president Vladimir Putin’s envoy. Trump revealed that he had an unscheduled meeting with Kirill Dmitriev, who was at the White House for talks with Ukrainian officials hosted by US first lady Melania Trump. “I can’t tell you what I discussed, but I’m just telling you, it’s going to be an agreement, it’s going to be a big agreement,” the US president told reporters in the Oval Office. “It’s going to be very big. It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe … everyone’s going to be thrilled.” Trump said he had not met with Ukrainian officials who were also at the White House on Thursday. His comments will fuel European concerns that he is pivoting towards the Kremlin and will pressure Ukraine towards an unfavourable deal to end Russia’s invasion.

Russia and Ukraine exchanged overnight airstrikes and one of Russia’s largest oil refineries appeared to have ⁠come under attack as a second day of talks on Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and security guarantees wrapped up in Brussels on Thursday. A Ukrainian attack on a bus killed five people and wounded 13 in Ukraine’s Russian-occupied Luhansk region, according to its Moscow-backed leader, Leonid Pasechnik. In Komyshuvakha, near the frontline in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, rescue teams continued searching for more than 30 people believed trapped in the wreckage of a former school and a nearby shelter hit by Russian guided bombs on Monday. Zelenskyyy said 43 people had been confirmed dead, also saying one person previously reported missing had been found alive. In Russia, the Ryazan oil refinery appeared to have ⁠come under attack as part of a large overnight drone strike on industrial sites in the city south-east of Moscow, according to a Reuters video analysis.

Russia arranged to supply Iran with 90 launchers for advanced guided missiles, according to leaked defence industry documents that shed light on the depth of military cooperation between Moscow and Tehran. Pjotr Sauer reports that the documents, obtained by a Ukrainian private intelligence firm and shared with the Guardian, detail plans to supply Iran with launchers for the LMUR, a guided missile fired from attack helicopters which Russian forces have used extensively against Ukraine.

Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni has slammed Europe’s “disorderly” approach to Ukraine negotiations and demanded the EU decide who speaks on its behalf, in a letter seen by Agence France-Presse. In the message to European Council chief António Costa, Meloni complained about the recent proliferation of meetings in different formats for talks on Russia’s war on Ukraine. “All this is making us look utterly lacking in credibility in handling one of the most complicated dossiers our nations are facing,” the Italian leader wrote. In response Costa wrote back that he agreed “Europe needs to act with coherence, unity and determination”.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
item.description:
President urges US for support, saying ‘Ukraine must not be left to face this alone’ as barrage plunges cities into darkness. What we know on day 1,719

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at upcoming talks after an overnight barrage triggered power cuts as temperatures drop. “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners,” the Ukrainian president said. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression.”

Ukraine’s energy ministry said “a massive attack on a number of energy facilities” on Saturday had plunged five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia had throughout the night launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, among which were KN-23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea.

The strikes came before a US-brokered trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi scheduled for next week aimed at reviving stalled diplomatic efforts towards peace. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and US envoys on Tuesday and Wednesday for the first such talks in months. The diplomatic track has been stalled since February when Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran.

Zelenskyy also urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine. “Unfortunately, there is still a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it,” he said.

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, on Saturday said he had been targeted by pro-Russian hackers over his backing for Ukraine. Tajani said in a post on X that “backing in a transparent way the freedom and independence of a sovereign state” had made him a target. Tajani said his personal data had been published on the dark web and that the hackers were seeking further information about him and his family and were ‌willing to pay for it.

The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who has been one of the strongest backers of Ukraine among western leaders, expressed her support for Tajani and said the sale of confidential information relating to public officials was “a matter of serious concern”. Moscow has not commented ‌on the incident. ‌

France’s far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Saturday that settling the Ukraine conflict could not be done by granting territorial concessions without consulting the people concerned. Melenchon, who polls suggest could reach the second round of next year’s presidential election, set out his France Unbowed party’s foreign policy positions at a rally just outside Paris.

Mélenchon has been criticised in the past for questioning the legitimacy of Zelenskyy. But in a campaign speech to thousands of supporters, he said an administration run by his party would take an active role in settling the war in Ukraine. Europe would have to play an active role in peace talks, he said. “We cannot accept that one could consider a peace with territorial concessions in Ukraine without asking the populations concerned if they agree or not to be on one side or other of the border,” he said. “It is for the people themselves to decide what they want,” he added.

A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said on Saturday. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, it said. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: post war ‘security guarantees’ a key focus in upcoming Abu Dhabi talks, says Rubio
item.description:
US secretary of state says some progress made on what security infrastructure could look like in Ukraine and Europe after the war. What we know on day 1,720

US secretary of state Marco Rubio said some progress had been made on what the “security infrastructure” of Ukraine and Europe could look like after the war with Russia, adding that talks this week could lead to further advances. Rubio’s comments on Sunday, ahead of his travel to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, come as Russia-Ukraine negotiations under US mediation have been set for Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump’s son-in-law, will represent the US in Abu Dhabi.

In an interview ‌with CBS’s “60 Minutes” broadcast on Sunday, Trump said he believed the war would end ‌soon and suggested Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered borders. “I think we’re gonna have it done, and I think it’s gonna happen and they’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine,” Trump said. Asked whether Russian president Vladimir Putin was stringing him along, Trump replied: “Oh, I don’t think so.”

On Sunday, Rubio said the whole time the US had been talking about Russia and Ukraine, “the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees” and what they would look like in Ukraine, and on the European continent. “I think that’s what the president’s alluding to – is that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture could look like post-conflict.”

French ⁠Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Europe would be well represented at the talks. “France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in ⁠these discussions,” Barrot told French radio station RTL. “I can’t ​tell you yet who will be ‌representing France on this ‌occasion, but France will certainly be there,” he added.

A Russian drone has struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine. Authorities say the attack on Sunday hit a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, previously targeted by Russian bombs. Ukraine said last Monday’s attack killed at least 55 people. No injuries were reported in Sunday’s strike but rescue equipment was damaged. About 50 people remain missing.

Power has been restored to the Russian-controlled ⁠Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine, hours after the plant lost its external electricity ⁠supply and had ⁠to ​use backup generators for reactor cooling, the UN’s nuclear watchdog said on Sunday. Zaporizhzhia, which does ⁠not produce electricity but needs power supplied by two external links to keep nuclear fuel cool, lost ⁠its off-site electricity supply earlier on Sunday after the Ferosplavna power ​line disconnected. The International Atomic ‌Energy Agency said the cause and location of the disconnection were unknown. The loss of power was the plant’s 27th such incident since the beginning of the conflict.

Russia said ⁠on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels ⁠that were carrying military ⁠goods ​for Ukraine and two electricity substations, which it said supplied power to ⁠the Ukrainian defence industry, Reuters reports. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering ⁠weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea ​port of Odesa, ‌and another in ‌the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same ‌southwestern region of Ukraine. According to the ministry, the second container ship had delivered dual-use cargo to Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, ‌was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.

Moldova on Sunday launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid, to reduce its reliance on Russian energy. “For decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us,” President Maia Sandu wrote on X. “No more. Moldova buys zero Russian gas.” Achieving energy security is a priority for the former Soviet republic of 2.6 million people, which has faced difficulties since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

item.title: ‘I am deeply sorry’: Nvidia stock falls as Jensen Huang’s affair and an alleged spying scandal rocks the AI industry
item.description:
Shares in Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA) are sinking today, less than 12 hours after CEO Jensen Huang publicly confirmed that he’d had an extramarital affair, and after the chipmaker confirmed that it was investigating Huang’s relationship amid reports that the woman he’d had an affair with was allegedly spying on behalf of Beijing.

The story has rocked the AI industry at a time when related tech stocks are already facing their most significant headwinds since the artificial intelligence boom first took off. Here’s everything you need to know to get caught up.

Huang and Nvidia confirm affair and investigation

Last night, Nvidia published a statement from its board of directors confirming that the company has launched an independent investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang.

The statement came following earlier reports by the New York Times and the Financial Times alleging that Huang had been having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a senior leader at a Singapore-based cloud company called Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence services believe the woman was spying on behalf of China, the reports said.

Nvidia makes the world’s most advanced chips and graphics cards, which are now the backbone of the AI revolution.

For years, the company’s most state-of-the-art technology has faced export restrictions to China over national security fears. The United States and China are locked in an AI arms race, and U.S. lawmakers and national security experts worry that the sale of Nvidia’s hardware to China would give the country an edge economically and militarily.

While the extramarital affair stands to damage Huang’s personal reputation, AI industry insiders, Wall Street, and security experts are most concerned about the fact that Huang’s companion may have also been working as an intelligence operative.

There are fears that any industry information or Nvidia secrets that Jensen Huang may have discussed with Alice Huang could have been passed along to foreign intelligence services.

After Huang confirmed the affair—and Nvidia confirmed the investigation—Nvidia’s stock sank in premarket trading on Monday. This is more bad news for investors who have already seen AI-related stocks get hammered in the past week.

Fast Company reached out to Megaspeed for comment. It was not immediately clear if Alice Huang, who could not be reached for comment, still worked there.

What has Jensen Huang said?

When reports of the affair first broke, Jensen Huang suggested that he’d had only had normal business engagements with Alice Huang. The two had been photographed together at multiple business and social events.

But last night, Huang sent an email to Nvidia employees confirming the affair. Nvidia later published the message on its website. 

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” the message began. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Addressing Nvidia employees directly, Huang said, “you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Huang also addressed the national security concerns about his affair, saying the company had launched an independent investigation.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang added.

Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993, has been seen as one of the single most influential tech leaders behind the AI revolution.

What has Nvidia said?

Nvidia confirmed that its board of directors has initiated an independent investigation into the reports that Huang may have “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” 

The investigation will be led by “independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel,” according to the company, with the board noting that it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

The company also stated that its board of directors has no reason to believe the company’s secrets or national security were compromised. 

Nvidia says that it still has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

What have China and the U.S. said?

Officials in China were quick to dispute the reports that it targeted Nvidia’s CEO in any way. Reuters quoted Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun as saying, “The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear.”

As for U.S. officials, when reporters asked Secretary of State Marco Rubio about the matter, he replied: “Yeah, I can’t comment on any of that. I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.  And I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.”

President Trump told reporters, “I have not spoken to [Jensen Huang] about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on.” He added: ”I hope everything’s fine.”

The president also said, “I think he’s an honorable guy,” noting that the Nvidia CEO had “done an amazing job for our country.”

How has NVDA stock reacted?

Not well. As of this writing, in premarket trading, Nvidia shares are down more than 5% to just above $177. If today’s premarket drop holds, Nvidia will have lost more than 26% of its value in the past month alone.

Like many AI-related stocks last week, Nvidia shares sank in the days after the 2026 U.S. midterm election results, amid fears that the incoming Democratic-led Congress would take a more cautious approach to AI data center buildouts than the current administration. Voters have overwhelmingly shown their distaste for the massive server farms.

Huang’s scandal is sure to do no favors to the larger AI industry, which is already facing worries about a stock market bubble and growing unpopularity with the broader public.

What happens next?

Nvidia likely won’t be the only entity investigating the allegations.

Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co, told CNBC, “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”

Ives believes there is a risk Jensen could be removed from his CEO position at Nvidia. 

“[T]his will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.”

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: battlefield gains bolstering Kyiv’s hand in US-led peace talks, Zelenskyy says
item.description:
Ukrainian president says battlefield successes and mounting Russian losses add to negotiating leverage ahead of Abu Dhabi talks on Tuesday. What we know on day 1,721

Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy has said ⁠that ​battlefield ‌successes ‌were strengthening Kyiv’s position ‌in negotiations, on ⁠the ⁠eve of ​new US-led trilateral talks ⁠on resolving the war. “Every ​task that is fully accomplished, every ⁠defensive operation that increases ​Ukraine’s strength ​and ​delivers results, strengthens ​Ukraine ‌and, above ​all, ​strengthens us in negotiations,” the president said in his nightly video address on Monday. Zelenskyy said ​top Ukrainian military commander Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented ‌a report that underscored heavy recent losses by Russian forces. He added that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on ‌Russian targets, including oil industry sites, were also working.

Russia’s battlefield losses have reached levels unprecedented in its modern history, according to data shared with the Guardian’s Pjotr Sauer. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine over nearly five years of fighting, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat. The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, shows 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.

US negotiators in Tuesday’s Abu Dhabi talks believe that Zelenskyy and Russian president Vladimir Putin may be willing to strike a compromise on ‌the vital question of territory, with each ceding a little, an American official told Reuters. Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to accession to the EU. In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on Sunday, Donald Trump said Ukraine would have “a little bit different shape” under the settlement, but he didn’t elaborate. A senior Ukrainian official strongly denied that the government would consider any such concessions.

Trump on Monday said that Washington was seeing ​a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting.” However, US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave a more sober assessment of peace efforts. Rubio said the process still has “ways to go”, and that getting Europeans to the table with the Russians has still not happened. “It’s been difficult to get anything productive out of that,” Rubio told reporters a day before the talks.

European powers, ⁠including France, Germany and the European Commission, ⁠will send officials to the talks, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations. Instead, Ukrainian delegates will meet separately to brief their European allies on progress. “We are doing everything to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process,” Rustem Umerov, the head of the Ukrainian delegation, said on Monday.

EU foreign ministers pressed Rubio at a G7 meeting in Paris to ensure Europe is represented at the negotiations. German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said after talks with Rubio: “Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe.” Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday that Trump’s team had placed “collective security”, covering not just Russia and Ukraine but also a wider area, at the top of the agenda.

Russian forces targeted four electrical substations in Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, Russia’s defence ministry said Monday. The attacks are part of Russia’s campaign to deny Ukrainian civilians heating, light and running water during the approaching winter. Zelenskyy said Monday the EU had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power grid repairs. Russian forces also hit a warehouse in Odesa in south-western Ukraine containing food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said.

A long-range Ukranian drone attack started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest, close to St. Petersburg, Leningrad governor Alexander Drozdenko said on Monday. Ukrainian forces also struck a plant near St. Petersburg, Russia’s second-largest city, that produces solid rocket propellant for Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Ukraine’s general staff said.

item.title: PepsiCo layoffs: 1,000 jobs reportedly slashed as CEO pushes soda giant to ‘be faster’ and ‘more capable’
item.description:
November has already been a tough month for layoffs.

In the tech sector, numerous big-name companies, including Amazon, Block, and Squarespace, have already cut roles or are planning to. But workplace reductions are not limited to just tech.

Yesterday, soft drink giant PepsiCo, Inc. (Nasdaq: PEP) reportedly announced that it will lay off around 1,000 employees in North America as sales in the region underperform. Here’s what you need to know.

Pepsi tells employees to prepare for job cuts

PepsiCo CEO Ram Krishnan wrote to employees stating that the company will cut around 1,000 positions in North America in the coming days, multiple media outlets reported.

In the email Krishnan sent to employees (per CNBC), the Pepsi boss said the company’s ambitions were to “build a stronger, more future-fit business that delivers industry-leading growth” in North America.

He added: “To do that, we need to be faster, more connected, and more capable, while continuing to invest in growth — behind our people, capabilities and brands.”

Unfortunately, the endeavor also involves layoffs.

“We will simplify how we operate, better connect teams and strengthen the capabilities we need,” Krishnan wrote. “The goal is to move faster, execute better and invest behind the opportunities that will drive our growth.” The Wall Street Journal first reported the layoffs.

The layoffs will be limited to Pepsi’s North American workforce, which includes roughly 125,000 positions in the United States.

Worldwide, Pepsi employs about 306,000 people as of the end of last year. The layoffs will reportedly happen over the coming week.

Fast Company reached out to PepsiCo for comment.

Pepsi’s North American sales lag other global markets

Last month, Pepsi announced its Q3 2026 financial results, which were broadly respectable. Net revenue increased 5.6%, and operating profit increased 19%.

As CNBC reported at the time, the company’s $25.27 billion in revenue for the quarter exceeded street expectations of $24.96 billion, and its adjusted EPS of $2.34 exceeded the $2.29 analysts had expected.

But Pepsi’s relatively positive results largely came from its international markets, which, year-to-date, have accounted for 41% of its net revenue.

In Pepsi’s home territory of North America, things are less rosy.

The North American food division of Pepsi, which includes products like Frito-Lay snacks, saw volume remain flat, while its beverage business volume declined by 2%.

The lackluster results in North America led Pepsi to reduce its core earnings per share expectations for the full 2026 fiscal year. Previously, Pepsi had expected growth of 5% to 7%. Now it expects growth of 2.5% to 3.5%.

When it came to Pepsi’s North American snacks results, the company blamed the lackluster demand on “the consumer environment.”

Pepsi stock loses its fizz

Pepsi’s North American numbers are the only thing going flat. The company’s share price has lost its fizz over the course of 2026. 

PEP stock began the year performing strongly: By late February, shares were up over 20% since the year began. But since a high above $170 reached in early 2026, Pepsi shares have declined significantly. 

As of yesterday’s close, PEP stock traded at $141. While its share price has increased more than 12% over the past 30 days, that recovery has not been enough to erase the mid-year losses.

As of yesterday’s close, PEP shares were down 1.1% for the year. The broader S&P 500 is up more than 10% over that same period.

But if Pepsi executives hoped layoffs could quickly boost the company’s stock price, they’ll be disappointed. While investors tend to cheer layoffs, since cutting jobs is often the easiest way to quickly improve the bottom line, they seem to have shrugged off the news.

Since the job cuts became public yesterday, PEP shares have hardly moved. Yesterday, Pepsi stock closed up just under four-tenths of a percent, and today in premarket trading, shares are up about the same amount as of the time of this writing.

item.title: DOJ sues Lyft for allegedly denying rides to people with disabilities
item.description:
The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on rideshare services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”

Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for the treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one — or, in some cases, several — drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.

“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The DOJ said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

—Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press

item.title: The Children’s Place is closing stores, joins list of struggling retailers to file for bankruptcy in 2026
item.description:
The Children’s Place (Nasdaq: PLCE), a popular children’s clothing retailer with around 500 locations, has announced it is filing for bankruptcy.

The news comes as the company has struggled for years with declining sales and higher costs—not to mention a falling stock price. Yet, for now at least, the company says it plans to keep operating if possible, while also noting that some of its stores will close. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

This week, The Children’s Place Inc. filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey.

In the filing, the company listed assets of approximately $742.3 million and debts of approximately $881.3 million on the books.

The filing comes just months after the company reported its Q2 2026 financial results in mid-September. Those results, which covered the period up to August 1, showed significant sales declines. 

In Q2, The Children’s Place posted revenue of $241.8 million, an 18.9% decline from the same quarter a year earlier. Gross profits fell to $83.3 million from $101.3 million for the same quarter a year earlier. 

The company reported it had 514 stores open at the end of the quarter, an increase of 19 stores from the previous quarter. It also operates an online storefront.

At the time, the company said comparables weighed on the results, particularly because “last year’s [2025] strong back-to-school demand was uniquely elevated by customer demand ahead of anticipated tariff price increases, which skewed those financial results compared to this year’s.”

Announcing the bankruptcy this week, The Children’s Place says it intends to “pursue a value-maximizing sale transaction” with the goal of selling “substantially all of its assets.”

The retailer is now seeking bids from interested parties by December 9, and if it receives any, expects to sell to a new buyer by the end of December.

Are The Children’s Place stores closing?

Unfortunately, some of them will. Though The Children’s Place is putting on its best face and insisting it wants to see the retail chain continue operating under new ownership, it also says that, even if that happens, some stores will be closing.

The company states that it “has been evaluating its operational footprint to invest its resources in its strongest locations moving forward” and “has determined that certain store closures will be necessary during the chapter 11 process.”

However, as of the time of this writing, all The Children’s Place locations and its online store are still open. Currently, the company’s website displays a large banner advertising a “total inventory blowout” on all in-store and online items. It adds that all sales are final.

Where does The Children’s Place have stores?

As of the end of Q2, The Children’s Place said it had 514 locations. Those locations include stores in the United States, Canada, Bahrain, Israel, Mexico, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Venezuela.

The company so far has not disclosed which locations will close as part of the bankruptcy process.

In the United States, the largest number of The Children’s Place stores are located in California, with 50 locations. It also has a significant number of stores in Florida and New York.

PLCE stock craters in 2026

The Children’s Place was founded in 1969 and went public in 1997. In 2018, the company’s stock price hit an all-time high of more than $161 per share. But since about 2021, the company’s stock price has steadily declined, and in 2026 it has cratered.

In January, the company’s stock price hit a 2026 high of around $5.09 per share. But since the beginning of the year, its stock price has now declined more than 95%. 

As of the time of this writing, the PLCE stock price is just 18 cents.

“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” António Guterres said, in a dramatic intervention on the second day of the conference on Tuesday.

item.title: US prosecutors charge Iranian operative allegedly responsible for UK air force base attack
item.description:
New indictment claims Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in US custody

US federal prosecutors have said that an Iranian operative jailed in New York was responsible for the foiled attack on a UK air force base where American B-1 bombers were stationed.

A new indictment alleged that Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in custody and then transmitted plans – using coded messages in calls to his family – to two co-conspirators to buy large quantities of chemicals that could be used as explosives in an attack on the RAF Fairford base in September.
